clinicalPearls: A haematocele is a collection of blood within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis, most often following scrotal trauma or surgery
It presents as a firm, tense, and often painful scrotal swelling that, unlike a simple hydrocele, does not transilluminate
A post-traumatic haematocele may be associated with an underlying testicular rupture, which must be actively excluded
Scrotal ultrasound is the key investigation to assess the integrity of the testis and characterise the collection
A tense or enlarging haematocele, or one associated with testicular rupture, is an indication for scrotal exploration, evacuation, and repair
Small collections with an intact testis may be managed conservatively with support, analgesia, and monitoring
A chronic, long-standing haematocele can become thick-walled and calcified and may compress and damage the testis over time
reference.pathophysiology: A haematocele forms when blood accumulates in the potential space between the layers of the tunica vaginalis. This most commonly follows blunt or penetrating scrotal trauma, sometimes with rupture of the tunica albuginea and extrusion of testicular tissue, but it may also arise after surgery, from bleeding into a pre-existing hydrocele, or spontaneously in the presence of a bleeding tendency or tumour. The trapped blood organises over time, and a chronic collection develops a thickened, sometimes calcified wall that can constrict the testis and impair its perfusion and function.
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound to assess testicular integrity and characterise the collection
Clinical assessment including transillumination (a haematocele does not transilluminate)
Coagulation studies if a bleeding tendency is suspected
Serum tumour markers when an underlying tumour is a concern
Scrotal exploration for diagnosis and treatment when rupture or a tense collection is present
redFlags: Suspected testicular rupture on ultrasound or examination
A tense, rapidly enlarging, or intensely painful collection
Signs of ongoing haemorrhage or haemodynamic compromise after major trauma
An underlying testicular tumour presenting with haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: With prompt exploration and repair of an associated testicular rupture, testicular salvage rates are good, whereas delayed management or a large chronic haematocele can lead to testicular atrophy or loss; small collections with an intact testis often resolve with conservative care.
pitfalls: Missing an underlying testicular rupture in a traumatic haematocele
Assuming a non-transilluminating swelling is a simple hydrocele
Delaying exploration of a tense post-traumatic collection
Overlooking a tumour as the source of spontaneous bleeding
Allowing a chronic haematocele to compress and atrophy the testis
management: Undertake urgent scrotal exploration with evacuation of the haematocele and repair of any testicular rupture, closing the tunica albuginea to maximise testicular salvage
Manage a small collection with an intact testis conservatively with scrotal support, rest, ice and analgesia under close monitoring
Actively exclude an underlying testicular rupture with scrotal ultrasound in all post-traumatic cases
Correct any bleeding tendency and investigate for an underlying tumour when there is no history of trauma
Follow up to detect an enlarging or organising chronic collection and secondary testicular atrophy
Refer promptly to urology, escalating tense, enlarging or rupture-associated collections to theatre
